title: The Magic in this Other World is Too Far Behind!
label: Quick read (from summaries)
premise: Suimei and his friends Reiji and Mizuki are summoned to a medieval-style kingdom to fight a demon invasion. Reiji accepts the hero role, but Suimei, a modern magician whose craft is far ahead of the local magic, refuses, calling the summoning a kidnapping, hides his power and looks for a way home to keep a promise to his late father.
life_message: Keep your promises and think for yourself instead of accepting the role others assign you.

content.note: Demon battles; the novel review notes harsh treatment of swordswoman Lefille (light novel; manga level to verify).
Harem-style love interests (MU Harem); MangaDex safe.
Grief for his father in the background.
Defying a king, framed as justified.

dominant: Refusing an imposed hero role; magic as rigorous science; promise to family

frames.aligns: Honoring a promise to a dead father; refusing to be used.
Questions misuse of power by a king.

frames.concerns: Summoning and magician hero open spiritual doors in this view.

frames.aligns: Duty to family over a borrowed vocation.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Suimei confronts the king in anger but hides his power to avoid fights.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Refuses the hero role the kingdom assigns him.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Promise to his father and his mother's need drive him home.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Treats a king as accountable, not owed obedience.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Magic treated as a rigorous, technical discipline.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Personal goals balanced against survival in a war.

folkways.japan: Suimei's duty to a dead father and his family echoes Japanese filial obligation within a standard summoned-hero isekai.

delivery.evidence: ANN's novel review says Suimei angrily tells the king the summoning was wrong; the reviewer calls him right, not preachy.

personified.ideology: using outsiders to solve the kingdom's war

delivery.note: The hero states his objection outright, while his friend's choice to help is not mocked.

winners_losers: Suimei's independence gets sympathy; the kingdom that summoned outsiders is shown as at fault.
